questions.topic: Trigonometric substitution for a difference of squares
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a radical of a difference of squares with a sine substitution
questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral of the square root of 1 minus x squared, taken from x = 0 to x = 1/2. Report the value as a number only.

The check that does not use the substitution is to differentiate the proposed antiderivative one half of x times the radical plus the arcsine of x, which returns the radical itself, and evaluating that at the two ends gives the same pair of pieces in the other order.

options.text: the logarithm of x minus the square root of x squared plus 9, plus a constant
options.misconception: picks the branch whose derivative is the negative of the integrand

questions.topic: One step of integration by parts

The integral is then e to the power x times x minus 1, and evaluating that at the two ends gives e squared times 1 minus 1 times minus 1, which is e squared plus 1. Since e squared is 7.3890560989, the value is 8.3890561. Adaptive numerical quadrature of x times e to the power x from 0 to 2 returns 8.3890560989 as well, so the two routes agree. questions.topic: Two steps of integration by parts

questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral of x squared times e to the power x, taken from x = 0 to x = 1. Report the value as a number only.

With u equal to x squared the first pass leaves an integral of 2x times e to the power x, and applying the formula to that leaves an integral of 2 times e to the power x, whose antiderivative is 2 e to the power x. Substituting back, the whole antiderivative is e to the power x times the quantity x squared minus 2x plus 2. At x equal to 1 that bracket is 1, and at x equal to 0 it is 2, so the definite integral is e minus 2, which is 0.7182818. Adaptive numerical quadrature of x squared times e to the power x over 0 to 1 returns 0.7182818285, agreeing to the digits shown. The pattern x squared minus 2x plus 2 is not a coincidence: at each pass the new polynomial is the old one minus the derivative of the factor that was integrated out.
questions.hint: Apply the parts formula twice, keeping a running polynomial, then evaluate the single resulting expression at both limits.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Integrating a logarithm by parts
questions.learningObjective: integrate a natural logarithm by parts
questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral of the natural logarithm of x, taken from x = 1 to x equal to e. Report the value as a number only.
questions.explanation: The logarithm has no elementary antiderivative that a substitution can produce, so integrate by parts with u equal to the logarithm of x and dv equal to dx. The derivative of the logarithm is 1 over x, and the antiderivative of 1 is x, so the integral becomes x times the logarithm of x minus the integral of 1, which is x times the logarithm of x minus x. At the upper limit e, the logarithm is 1, so the value there is e minus e, which is 0. At the lower limit 1, the logarithm is 0, so the value there is 0 minus 1, which is minus 1. The definite integral is therefore 0 minus minus 1, which is 1. Numerical quadrature over the same interval returns 1.0000000000, so the two routes agree. The neatness of the answer comes from the choice of limits: they are the two points where the logarithm takes the values 0 and 1.
questions.hint: Take u equal to the logarithm and v equal to x, then use the two special values of the logarithm at 1 and at e.

questions.topic: Cyclic integration by parts
questions.learningObjective: close the loop when a parts choice returns to the original integral
questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral of e to the power x times the cosine of x, taken from x = 0 to x = pi over 2. Report the value as a number only.

The remaining integral is the same shape as the original with sine and cosine exchanged, so apply the formula a second time to it: that gives e to the power x times the sine of x minus the original integral again. Naming the original integral I, the two equations read I equals the boundary term minus the sine integral and the sine integral equals e to the power x times the sine of x minus I, and eliminating the sine integral leaves 2I equal to the boundary terms, which is e to the power x times the sine of x plus the cosine of x. Divided by 2, that antiderivative evaluates at pi over 2 as e to the power pi over 2 over 2 and at 0 as one half, giving one half of e to the power pi over 2 minus one half, which is 1.9052387. Numerical quadrature returns 1.9052386905, so the two routes agree.
questions.hint: Apply the parts formula twice, notice the second pass returns the original integral, and solve the resulting linear equation.

questions.topic: Repeated parts on a squared logarithm
questions.learningObjective: integrate a squared logarithm by applying parts twice
questions.stem: Evaluate the improper-looking but convergent integral of the square of the natural logarithm of x, taken from x = 0 to x = 1. The integrand is unbounded at the lower limit. Report the value as a number only.
questions.explanation: The integrand is unbounded at 0 but the integral converges, so it must be read as the limit from a positive lower cut-off, and the parts formula is applied to that. Take u equal to the square of the logarithm, so that du is 2 times the logarithm over x dx, and dv equal to dx, so v equals x. The integral becomes x times the square of the logarithm minus 2 times the integral of the logarithm, and the second integral was evaluated in the previous style as x times the logarithm minus x. Substituting that back gives an antiderivative of x times the square of the logarithm minus 2x times the logarithm plus 2x. As x goes to 0 every term here goes to 0, since x times any power of the logarithm vanishes faster than the logarithm grows, and at x equal to 1 the value is 2. The definite integral is therefore 2. Numerical quadrature of the same integrand over 0 to 1 returns 2.0000000000, so the two routes agree. The limit step is the part that must not be skipped, because the antiderivative is only defined for positive x.
questions.hint: Write the integral as a limit from a positive cut-off, integrate the logarithm by parts twice, and then take the cut-off to zero.

Parts applies, taking u equal to the exponential because its derivative simplifies the product into something shorter
options.misconception: applies parts to a product in which a substitution already resolves the whole integrand

questions.learningObjective: use additivity to split a definite integral at an interior point
questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral of x squared plus 2, taken from x = 0 to x = 3, by first splitting the interval at x = 1 and integrating the two pieces separately. Report the value as a number only.
questions.explanation: The additivity rule says that splitting the interval changes nothing about the value, provided both pieces converge, and here the integrand is a polynomial so convergence is not in question. The first piece, from 0 to 1, is the cube of 1 over 3 plus 2 times 1, which is 7 over 3. The second piece, from 1 to 3, is 27 over 3 minus 1 over 3 plus 2 times 2, which is 26 over 3 plus 4, that is 38 over 3. Adding gives 45 over 3, which is 15. Integrating the whole interval in one pass gives 9 plus 6, also 15, so the two routes agree. The reason the rule is worth stating is that it is what licenses every later trick built on symmetry: a symmetric interval is really two pieces glued at the origin, and oddness says those two pieces have opposite values.
questions.hint: Evaluate the two pieces separately with the polynomial antiderivative and add them; the single-pass computation should agree.

questions.topic: Even integrand on a symmetric interval
questions.learningObjective: use even symmetry to halve a definite integral and double the result
questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral of 3x squared plus 1, taken from x = -2 to x = 2. The integrand is even, so use that. Report the value as a number only.
questions.explanation: An even function takes the same value at opposite points, so over an interval symmetric about the origin the two halves contribute equally and the whole integral is twice the half integral. Here that gives twice the integral from 0 to 2 of 3x squared plus 1, which is twice the quantity 3 times 8 over 3 plus 2, that is twice 10, which is 20. Integrating straight across gives the same figure: 3 times 16 over 3 plus 4, again 20. The error this rule exists to prevent is halving the result, that is reporting 10, which forgets to double the half back up, and the reason it is a real error rather than a cosmetic one is that the half integral is not the answer to the question asked.
questions.hint: Double the integral over the positive half; the same number should come out of a single pass across the whole interval.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Odd integrand on a symmetric interval
questions.learningObjective: recognise that an odd integrand cancels over a symmetric interval
questions.stem: A student is asked for the definite integral of x cubed plus x from -2 to 2 and answers 4, arguing that the part below the axis contributes nothing. Which correction is right, and what is the value?

options.text: The value is 4, since the part below the axis is negative and a definite integral records only the area swept out
options.misconception: claims a definite integral ignores sign while insisting on a nonzero value

options.text: The value is 6, which is the integral over the positive half, since the negative half is what must be discarded
options.misconception: reports the half integral while describing a different reason for dropping the other half

options.text: The value is 12, which is twice the positive half, since both halves lie above the axis for this integrand
options.misconception: asserts that the integrand is positive below the origin, which it is not

options.text: The value is 0, because an odd integrand on a symmetric interval produces equal and opposite contributions that cancel

questions.explanation: The integrand x cubed plus x is odd, since replacing x by its negative negates it, and the interval from -2 to 2 is symmetric about the origin. The contributions from the two halves therefore have equal magnitude and opposite sign, and the value is exactly 0. The positive half contributes 4 plus 2, which is 6, and the negative half contributes minus 6, so the two cancel exactly. A definite integral is a signed area, not a geometric area, which is the belief behind the student's answer of 4: nothing about a definite integral discards negative contributions. The difference between 0 and the geometric area of the region is exactly the area under the curve on the positive half, which is 6.
questions.hint: Test whether the integrand is odd by replacing x with minus x, then use symmetry over the interval centred at the origin.

questions.topic: Reversing the limits reverses the sign
questions.learningObjective: explain why exchanging the limits of a definite integral changes its sign
questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral of the square root of x, taken with the lower limit 2 and the upper limit 0, that is with the limits written in that order. Report the value as a number only.
questions.explanation: Exchanging the limits negates the value, because the definite integral is defined as an antiderivative evaluated at the upper limit minus its value at the lower limit, and swapping the two terms changes the sign of the difference. The antiderivative of the square root of x is two thirds of x to the power three halves, and the two thirds of 2 to the three halves is 1.8856181, so the integral from 2 to 0 is minus 1.8856181. For a concrete picture, the integral from 0 to 2 is the area under an increasing curve above the axis, a positive quantity, and reversing the limits is what makes the value negative, not any change in the region being swept. The integrand is undefined below 0, so the interval cannot be pushed any further in the negative direction.
questions.hint: Write the antiderivative at the upper limit minus the antiderivative at the lower limit, with the limits exactly as given.

questions.topic: Substitution that rescales the limits
questions.learningObjective: carry a constant factor from the differential into the value
questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral of e to the power 4x, taken from x = 0 to x = 1/2. Report the value as a number only.

The integral becomes one quarter of the integral of e to the power u from 0 to 2, which is one quarter of e squared minus 1. Since e squared is 7.3890560989, the value is one quarter of 6.3890560989, which is 1.5972640. Adaptive numerical quadrature of e to the power 4x over 0 to 0.5 returns 1.5972640247, so the two routes agree. Forgetting it gives 6.3890561, which is four times too large.
questions.hint: Substitute for 4x, remember the reciprocal of the scale factor sits in front, and let the limits stretch from 0 to 2.

questions.topic: Integrands that vanish over a full period
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a trigonometric integral over a complete period
questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral of 1 plus 2 times the cosine of x plus 3 times the cosine of 2x, taken from x = 0 to x = 2pi. Report the value as a number only.
questions.explanation: Every term in the integrand is periodic with period 2pi, or a divisor of it, so a full period is exactly the interval of integration. The constant term contributes 2pi, and both cosine terms contribute nothing, because the integral of the cosine of kx from 0 to 2pi is the sine of 2kpi over k, which is 0 for every positive integer k. So the value is 2pi, which is 6.2831853. The check that does not rely on recognising periodicity is direct antiderivative evaluation: 2x plus 2 sine of x plus 3 over 2 sine of 2x, taken from 0 to 2pi, where the sine terms vanish at both ends and the constant term contributes 4pi minus 0. Splitting the interval into two halves and integrating each separately gives the same 6.2831853, confirming that the two halves each contribute half.
questions.hint: Integrate term by term; both cosine terms vanish over a full period and only the constant survives.

questions.topic: Repeated periods of a squared function
questions.learningObjective: count the periods in an interval before integrating a squared function
questions.stem: Consider the function whose square is the sine squared of x. First report the value of the integral of the sine squared of x from 0 to pi, then report the value of the integral of the sine squared of x from 0 to 3pi. Report the second value only.

options.misconception: computes a single period and forgets that the interval holds three of them
credits each period with pi instead of the correct pi over 2, doubling the total
treats the length 2 pi of a period as though it were the value of the integral over it

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: An absolute value over a full period
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the area under a non-negative periodic integrand
questions.stem: The definite integral of the absolute value of the cosine of x, taken from 0 to 2pi, is the area of a non-negative periodic integrand over a full period. Which of the following is that area?

options.text: 4.0000, being four times the quarter-period integral of the cosine, which is 1
0.0000, being the integral of the cosine over a full period, where the cancellation is exact
options.misconception: drops the absolute value and integrates a function that changes sign

options.text: 2.0000, being two quarter-periods rather than the four the function actually completes
options.misconception: counts half as many quarter periods as the curve actually traces

options.text: 6.2832, being the length of the interval multiplied by the average value 1 of the integrand
options.misconception: assumes the average height is 1, but the average of the absolute cosine is 2 over pi

questions.explanation: The absolute value of the cosine is positive on the first quarter period, negative in sign but positive in value on the second, and repeats twice over the full interval, so there are four quarter periods each contributing the same area. On each quarter period the absolute value of the cosine equals the cosine itself, and the integral of the cosine from 0 to pi over 2 is 1. Four times 1 is 4. The average value of the integrand is 4 divided by 2pi, which is 2 over pi and is about 0.6366, not 1, so the length times 1 route is wrong. Dropping the absolute value gives 0 because the two halves cancel, which measures a signed area rather than the area the question asks for. The independent check is that the four quarter-period areas are all equal, so any one of them times four is the answer.
questions.hint: Count the quarter periods over which the absolute value equals the cosine itself, and note that each contributes an area of 1.

questions.topic: An even integrand built from an absolute value
questions.learningObjective: establish even symmetry for an integrand containing an absolute value
questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral of e to the power of the absolute value of x, taken from x = -1 to x = 1. The integrand is even even though it contains an absolute value. Report the value as a number only.

Splitting the interval at the origin and integrating the two pieces with the absolute value resolved on each gives the same number: on the negative half the integrand is e to the power of minus x, whose antiderivative is minus e to the power of minus x, evaluated from minus 1 to 0 it is minus 1 plus e, that is 1.7182818285, matching the positive half. The reason the evenness is worth checking rather than assuming is that an absolute value inside an exponent looks like it might break the symmetry, and here it does not.
questions.hint: Check whether the function of the absolute value is even, and if so double the integral over the positive half.

questions.topic: Recognising the chain rule in reverse
questions.learningObjective: recognise a derivative of a composite function inside an integrand
questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral of x times the cosine of x squared, taken from x = 0 to x = 1. Report the value as a number only.

The limits 0 and 1 become 0 and 1, and the answer is one half of the sine of 1, which is 0.4207355. questions.topic: A substitution after splitting an odd power
questions.learningObjective: split an odd power so the remaining differential matches a substitution
questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral of x cubed times the quantity x squared plus 1 raised to the fifth power, taken from x = 0 to x = 1. Report the value as a number only.
questions.explanation: The exponent 5 on the bracket and the cubic outside are a trap, because a reader may expect to substitute for the bracket and find a leftover power of x. Split the cubic first: x cubed is x squared times x, and x squared is the bracket minus 1. With u equal to x squared plus 1 the differential is 2x dx, so the integral becomes one half of the integral of u minus 1 times u to the fifth from 1 to 2, which is one half of the integral of the sixth power minus the fifth power. That antiderivative is one half of u to the seventh over 7 minus u to the sixth over 6, evaluated from 1 to 2. At 2 the bracket is 128 over 7 minus 64 over 6, and at 1 it is 1 over 7 minus 1 over 6, and the difference is 107 over 28, which is 3.8214286. Adaptive numerical quadrature of the original integrand over 0 to 1 returns 3.8214285714, so the two routes agree. Without splitting the cubic, a reader would see a leftover x and wrongly reach for a second substitution.
questions.hint: Split the cubic so that one x pairs with the differential of the bracket, and rewrite the remaining x squared as the bracket minus 1.

With u equal to the logarithm of x, so that du is dx over x, and the outer substitution v equal to the logarithm of u, so that dv is du over u, the integral becomes the integral of dv, which is v. Reading the constants back, the antiderivative is the logarithm of the logarithm of x. At the upper limit e squared the logarithm is 2, so the value is the logarithm of 2, which is 0.6931471806. At the lower limit the square root of e the logarithm is one half, so the value is the logarithm of one half, which is minus 0.6931471806. The difference is 1.3862944. What is the area under this graph between 0 and 6?

options.text: 4.5, being the area of one of the two triangles the V is built from, since the two halves mirror each other
options.misconception: computes a single triangle and forgets that the V contributes a second congruent one

options.text: 6, being the product of the base 6 and the maximum height 1 read off the vertical axis
options.misconception: reads the peak height as 1 when the labelled peak is 3

18, being the area of the bounding rectangle of width 6 and height 3 with the corners counted twice

questions.learningObjective: split a definite integral where the expression under a root changes sign
questions.stem: Consider the integral of the square root of the absolute value of x minus 3, taken from x = 0 to x = 4. First name the value of x at which the integrand changes formula, then report the value of the integral. Report the value only.

options.misconception: handles only the piece to the left of the corner, which is 2 times the square root of 3
handles only the piece to the right of the corner, which is two thirds
handles the left piece and then doubles it, which gives 4 times the square root of 3

questions.explanation: Stage one, the integrand changes formula at x equal to 3, where the expression under the root vanishes. Stage two, the left piece is the integral from 0 to 3 of the root of 3 minus x, which is two thirds of 3 to the three halves, that is 2 times the square root of 3, or 3.4641016. The right piece is the integral from 3 to 4 of the root of x minus 3, which is two thirds of 1, that is 0.6666667. The total is 2 times the square root of 3 plus two thirds, which is 4.1307683. The numerical check that catches the truncated routes is adaptive quadrature over the whole interval, which returns 4.1307682818, and it matches the sum of the two pieces exactly while matching neither piece alone. The reason the right piece is so much smaller is that the corner value of the integrand is 0 and it only has one unit of horizontal room to grow.
questions.hint: Split at the corner where the expression under the root is zero, then integrate a root of a linear function on each side.

questions.topic: The square root of a square is an absolute value

questions.stem: A student writes that the definite integral of the square root of x squared from -2 to 3 equals 5 over 2, having replaced the radical by x because the square root of a square is the original function. What is the error, and what is the correct value?

options.text: The value is 6.5, because the square root of x squared is the absolute value of x, not x, and the negative half must be counted positively
The value is 5 over 2 is correct, because the identity the square root of a square is x holds for every real x
options.misconception: accepts a correct-looking answer from an identity that only holds where x is non-negative

options.text: The value is 35 over 3, because the radical should have been replaced by x squared rather than by x
options.misconception: raises the power instead of taking the root, producing a quartic region

options.text: The value is 0, because the square root of x squared is an even function and an even function integrates to zero
options.misconception: confuses evenness with vanishing integral, which belongs to oddness

questions.explanation: The square root of x squared equals the absolute value of x, not x, and the identity the square root of a square is x is valid only where x is non-negative. Over the interval from -2 to 3 the integrand is therefore minus x on the negative part and x on the positive part, so the integral is the integral of minus x from -2 to 0, which is 2, plus the integral of x from 0 to 3, which is 4.5, giving 6.5. The student's 2.5 is the integral of x across the whole interval, which ignores the sign flip at the origin. The claim that the answer is 0 confuses two symmetries: an even function over a symmetric interval gives twice the half integral, while an odd one gives zero, and the absolute value of x is even.
questions.hint: Replace the radical by the absolute value of x, then split the interval at the origin and integrate minus x on the left and x on the right.

questions.topic: An even index under a cube root

questions.explanation: A cube root behaves differently from an even root, and that difference is the point of the item. Because 3 is odd, the cube root of x squared is x to the power two thirds, and that expression is already non-negative for every real x, so no absolute value appears. The integrand is therefore the non-negative function whose value at 8 is 4 and whose value at 0 is 0. Integrating from 0 to 8 gives three fifths of 8 to the five thirds, and 8 to the five thirds is 32, so that piece is 19.2. Integrating from 0 to 1 gives three fifths, that is 0.6. The two pieces add, since the integrand is non-negative on both halves, giving 19.8. If the index were even the reader would have to insert an absolute value, and dropping it would change the answer by exactly twice the integral of x to the two thirds over the negative half.
questions.hint: Because the root index is odd, the radicand can be divided through to give a fractional power with no absolute value; integrate that on each half and add.

questions.topic: An absolute value whose turning point is interior

questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral of the absolute value of 2x minus 3, taken from x = 0 to x = 2. Report the value as a number only.

On the left the absolute value is 3 minus 2x, and on the right it is 2x minus 3. The left piece is 3x minus x squared evaluated at 3 over 2, which is 4.5 minus 2.25, that is 2.25. The right piece is x squared minus 3x from 3 over 2 to 2, which is 4 minus 6 minus 2.25 plus 4.5, that is 0.25. The total is 2.5. The two pieces are nowhere near equal, and the picture explains why: the graph starts at height 3 on the left endpoint, falls linearly to 0 at the corner 3 over 2, and climbs back only to height 1 at the right endpoint. The two triangles under it have base 1.5 and height 3, and base 0.5 and height 1, so the areas are 2.25 and 0.25. A reader who assumed the two arms were mirror images, which they are not because the interval is not centred on the corner, would get 3 instead.
questions.hint: Split at the interior root of the expression, integrate a linear function on each side, and check the picture against two unequal triangles.

questions.topic: Resolving an absolute value before integrating

The integral is therefore the integral of (x minus 1) times e to the power x, and integrating by parts with u equal to x minus 1 and dv equal to e to the power x dx gives the antiderivative e to the power x times the quantity x minus 2. At 2 that is 0, and at 1 it is minus e, so the definite integral is e, which is 2.7182818. Adaptive numerical quadrature of the original integrand over 1 to 2 returns 2.7182818285, so the two routes agree. The reason the answer comes out as e is structural: the factor x minus 1 is exactly the bracket that makes the antiderivative vanish at the upper limit, so the value is determined solely by the lower limit.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: What a constant of integration can absorb
questions.learningObjective: explain what happens to a constant of integration in a definite integral
questions.stem: A student finds the antiderivative of the cosine of x squared to be the sine of x squared over 2 plus a constant C, and then uses that formula to claim the definite integral from 0 to 1 must depend on the value of C chosen. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The value does depend on C, because a definite integral inherits whatever arbitrary term the antiderivative carries
options.misconception: believes the arbitrary constant survives the subtraction of the two endpoint evaluations

options.text: The value does not depend on C, but only after choosing C to be 0, which is the conventional and required choice
options.misconception: thinks cancellation requires setting the constant to zero rather than subtracting two copies of it

options.text: The value does not depend on C, because evaluating an antiderivative at two limits subtracts two copies of the same constant, which cancel
The value does depend on C, because the constant is needed to make the antiderivative match the integrand at every point
options.misconception: treats the constant as forced by the derivative condition rather than free

questions.explanation: Every antiderivative of a given function on an interval differs from every other by a constant, and a definite integral is computed by taking one antiderivative and subtracting its value at the upper limit from its value at the lower limit. Since the same C appears in both evaluations, it cancels exactly, and the definite integral is determined by the function alone. Nothing needs to be assumed about the value of C, and setting it to zero first is a convenience rather than a requirement. The condition that the derivative of the antiderivative equals the integrand places no restriction on C, since the derivative of a constant is zero; that is precisely why C is arbitrary. The distinction matters practically: an antiderivative is a family of functions, whereas a definite integral is a single number, and only the number survives.
questions.hint: Write out the two endpoint evaluations explicitly and look at where the constant appears in the subtraction.

options.text: 2, being the value of x alone, which is what remains when the logarithmic term is dropped
options.misconception: differentiates the quadratic and forgets the derivative of the logarithm

options.text: 1.3069, being the value of F itself at 2 rather than the value of its derivative there
options.misconception: reports the antiderivative instead of the integrand recovered from it

options.text: 1, being 2 minus 1, which treats the natural logarithm of 2 as though it were exactly 1
options.misconception: rounds the logarithm to an integer before subtracting

options.text: 1.5, being 2 minus one half, since the derivative is x minus one over x

Evaluating at 2 gives 2 minus one half, which is 1.5. This is the standard test for a proposed antiderivative and it works in both directions: if the derivative returns the integrand then the formula is correct up to a constant, and if it does not then the formula is simply wrong. The option reporting 1.3069 is the value of the antiderivative at 2, since 2 minus the logarithm of 2 is 1.3068528, and it is the classic confusion between a function and its rate of change. The option reporting 1 substitutes an integer for a logarithm, which is arithmetic carelessness rather than a calculus error, but it is worth naming as a distinct failure.
questions.hint: Differentiate the quadratic term and the logarithmic term separately, then evaluate the resulting expression at x equal to 2.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: The integral of an inverse function
questions.learningObjective: use the inverse-function area identity to avoid computing an antiderivative
questions.stem: Explain the identity that says the integral of a function from a to b plus the integral of its inverse from f of a to f of b equals b times f of b minus a times f of a, describe what the two integrals measure geometrically, and show on a worked example how the identity can replace a hard antiderivative with an easy one.

answer.exemplar: The identity is that the integral of f from a to b plus the integral of f inverse from f of a to f of b equals b f of b minus a f of a. Geometrically, the region under the curve from a to b splits into a rectangle of width b minus a and height f of a, and a second piece sitting above the line y equals f of a. The integral of the inverse counts that second piece from the other side, because integrating f inverse with respect to its own variable measures horizontal slices, and those horizontal slices of the same leftover region are exactly the vertical slices the first integral missed. What remains after both counts is the area of the bounding rectangle of width b minus a and height f of b minus f of a, and adding that rectangle's area to the lower rectangle of height f of a reproduces b f of b minus a f of a, which is the identity. The practical use is that one of the two integrals is usually much easier than the other. For the square root on the interval from 1 to 9, the antiderivative two thirds of y to the three halves is available, but taking the other route is shorter: the inverse of the square root is the square, so the integral of the square root from 1 to 9 equals 3 times 9 minus 1 times 1 minus the integral of x squared from 1 to 3, which is 26 minus 26 over 3, that is 52 over 3. That is a genuine saving, because the difficult direction was the one whose value was supplied by the identity rather than computed. The condition to keep in mind is that f must be continuous and one to one on the interval, so that the inverse exists as a single-valued function and the geometric argument applies; without that, the region counted by the second integral can overlap the first in a way the identity does not describe.

questions.explanation: The exemplar has to give the rectangle decomposition, since that is the part of the identity a reader cannot reconstruct from the formula alone, and it has to demonstrate the substitution of a hard integral for an easy one so the identity is used rather than merely stated. The final sentence records the hypotheses, because the identity fails when f is not one to one and that failure is exactly what makes the geometric picture wrong.
questions.hint: Draw the region under the curve, split it at the horizontal line through the value at the left endpoint, and note that the inverse integral counts the upper piece in the other direction.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Why the inverse-function identity holds
questions.learningObjective: explain the geometric content of the inverse-function area identity
questions.stem: The inverse-function identity pairs the integral of a function with the integral of its inverse on a matching interval. Why does the pairing produce a quantity that depends only on the four endpoint values and not on the shape of the curve in between?

options.text: The two integrals together cover the region exactly once, and the only part not covered by either is the corner rectangle, whose area is fixed by the endpoints
The two integrals together cover the region twice, and averaging them cancels every contribution that depends on the shape of the curve
options.misconception: believes the pairing works by averaging a doubly counted region rather than by tiling it once

options.text: The two integrals both depend only on the endpoints, because an integral of a monotone function is always determined by its limits
options.misconception: claims every integral of a monotone function is endpoint-determined, which is false

options.text: The two integrals are related by the fundamental theorem, so one is just a reparameterised copy of the other with no new information added
options.misconception: denies that the pairing gains information, treating the two integrals as redundant

questions.explanation: Integrating the function with respect to its argument sweeps the region under the curve in vertical strips, while integrating the inverse with respect to its own variable sweeps the region to the left of the curve in horizontal strips, and those two regions together fill the bounding rectangle apart from one corner piece. The corner piece is the rectangle of width b minus a and height f of b minus f of a, and its area depends on the four endpoint values only. Adding the two strips to that corner rectangle reproduces the full bounding rectangle, whose area is b f of b minus a f of a, and that is why the sum is free of the curve's shape. This is the same structural reason the trapezoid rule is exact for a straight line. What the identity does not do is make both integrals easy; exactly one of the two is likely to have a hard antiderivative, and that is the direction the identity is used to avoid.
questions.hint: Compare vertical strips with horizontal strips on the same region and identify which rectangle is left over.

questions.learningObjective: recognise a substitution whose differential is already a factor of the integrand
questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral of 3x squared times e to the power of x cubed, taken from x = 0 to x = 1. Report the value as a number only.
questions.explanation: The derivative of the exponent x cubed is 3x squared, and that is exactly the leading factor, so the substitution needs no extra constant at all. Put u equal to x cubed, so that du is 3x squared dx, and the limits 0 and 1 become 0 and 1. The integral is then the integral of e to the power u from 0 to 1, which is e minus 1, and since e is 2.7182818285 the value is 1.7182818. Differentiating the result confirms the setup: the derivative of e to the power x cubed is e to the power x cubed times 3x squared, which is the integrand. This is the cleanest possible instance of the pattern, and it is worth contrasting with the same integral when a factor of 3 is missing, since then the substitution leaves a leftover one third and the answer becomes one third of this value.
questions.hint: Check whether the leading factor is exactly the derivative of the function inside the exponent, and if so substitute for it.

questions.topic: The factor lost in a power reduction
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a missing constant when rewriting a squared sine with a cosine
questions.stem: A student rewrites the sine squared of x as one half of one minus the cosine of twice x, integrates from 0 to 2pi, and reports pi over 2. What is the error, and what is the correct value?

options.text: The value is pi over 2 is correct, since the factor of one half was applied to the whole antiderivative
options.misconception: accepts a result that dropped the constant term of the power reduction

options.text: The value is 2pi, being the length of the interval times the constant one half, since the cosine term contributes nothing
options.misconception: forgets to integrate the constant term and multiplies the height by the length instead

options.text: The value is pi, being 2pi minus 4, because the second cosine term integrates to 0 and only the constant half survives
The value is 0, being the integral of the sine itself rather than its square, which is what the reduction actually computes
options.misconception: replaces the squared integrand with the unsquared one and reports its vanishing integral

questions.explanation: The power reduction itself is correct, since the sine squared of x is indeed one half of one minus the cosine of twice x. The error is in integrating it: the constant term one half integrated from 0 to 2pi contributes one half times 2pi, which is pi, and the cosine term contributes the sine of 4pi over 2 minus the sine of 0, which is 0. So the value is pi, and the reported pi over 2 comes from integrating the constant one half as though the interval had length 1. A quick sanity check catches this: the integrand lies between 0 and 1 everywhere, so its integral over an interval of length 2pi must lie between 0 and 2pi, and 1.5708 is possible while 0 is not. The complementary reduction, one half of one minus the cosine of twice x, integrates to pi over 2 over a single period of length pi, which is the number the student should have used for the interval 0 to pi rather than for the full circle.
questions.hint: The reduction is right, so integrate both terms: the constant contributes one half times the length of the interval and the cosine contributes nothing.

questions.topic: When a substitution supplies no factor
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a substitution that leaves the integrand without the required factor
questions.stem: A student must evaluate the definite integral of x times e to the power of x squared from 0 to 1, chooses the substitution u equal to x squared, and reports that the integral equals e to the power 1 minus 1, reasoning that e to the power of u has antiderivative e to the power of u. What is the error, and what is the correct value?

options.text: The value is 1.4627, being the integral of e to the power of x squared itself, since the substitution is right and only the limits were misread
options.misconception: keeps the substitution but discards the leading factor of x from the integrand

options.text: The value is 1.7183, being e minus 1, since e to the power of u is the antiderivative and the differential contributed no extra factor
options.misconception: accepts the missing factor of one half and the discarded leading x as harmless

options.text: The value is 0, since after substituting nothing of the original integrand survives and the integral of a vanishing remainder is nothing
options.misconception: concludes that a leftover factor cancels the whole integrand rather than supplying part of it

options.text: The value is 0.8591, being one half of e minus 1, because the substitution gives dx as du over 2x and the leading x cancels one of the two

questions.explanation: The substitution u equal to x squared is the right idea, and the antiderivative of e to the power of u is right too, but the differential has to be carried through completely. Since du is 2x dx, the factor x dx is du over 2, and the remaining factor of x squared is the bracket minus 1, so the integrand becomes (u minus 1) times du over 2 rather than a bare du. The integral is therefore one half of the integral of e to the power of u, which is one half of e to the power of u, and the definite value is one half of e minus 1, that is 0.8591409. Numerical quadrature of the original integrand over 0 to 1 returns 0.8591409142, so the routes agree. The lesson is that a substitution replaces a differential, not an integrand, and any factor left over after the replacement has to be accounted for explicitly.
questions.hint: Carry the differential through: du is 2x dx, so the integrand becomes one half times x squared times e to the power of u, and x squared is u minus 1.
